content: For each variable collected, it is essential to ensure that the required information is obtained from all patients. For instance, if tuberculosis (TB) patients are to be stratified by their country of origin, every patient must be asked to provide this information. Similarly, if the decision is made to collect HIV status for all patients, a detailed protocol must be developed in accordance with national guidelines to ensure confidentiality and provide appropriate counseling for all individuals. A copy of the completed clinical information form should be sent to the coordination team, while the original form must remain at the diagnostic center. Ensuring the accuracy of patient classification as either new or previously treated for TB is critical, as this has significant implications for data analysis and interpretation. Special efforts must be made during surveys to ensure the reliability of clinical data. Clinical information forms should include specific questions to accurately capture patients' treatment histories. These forms must be carefully reviewed for deficiencies, and the reliability of the recorded information should be regularly assessed. Re-interviewing patients is a key method to verify treatment histories. For example, a representative sample of patients (typically 10%) can be re-interviewed by a designated member of the coordination team to evaluate the accuracy of recorded treatment histories. Additionally, all patients with rifampicin resistance, especially new patients, should be re-interviewed. Verification of treatment history is particularly important in settings where incentives are provided to staff for detecting new patients only, or where circumstances may encourage patients to falsify their treatment history. Measures should be taken to create a comfortable interview environment and eliminate barriers that may prevent patients from disclosing truthful treatment histories. Patients may be more willing to provide accurate treatment details once they begin feeling better after starting treatment. It is important to note that surveys often classify a higher proportion of cases as previously treated compared to routine programmatic records. This discrepancy arises because comprehensive patient treatment histories recorded during surveys reduce the likelihood of misclassification. The proper collection, processing, and rapid transportation of sputum samples to participating laboratories are essential to ensure accurate and reliable results. The number of samples required depends on the testing methods being used. Health care workers must be thoroughly trained to provide clear instructions to patients for collecting high-quality sputum samples. Since aerosols containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis may be generated when patients cough to produce sputum, samples should be collected either outdoors in open air or in specially designed sputum collection rooms with appropriate ventilation and/or methods to kill bacilli, such as ultraviolet irradiation. Sputum collection should not occur in confined spaces like laboratory rooms or toilets. Sputum samples must be handled with care. Containers should be rigid to prevent crushing during transit and equipped with watertight, wide-mouthed, screw-top lids to prevent leakage and contamination. Containers should be packed in absorbent material to mitigate leakage caused by accidents. Before transport, sputum samples should be stored in a cool place, preferably refrigerated at +4°C. Cool boxes should be used to transport samples from health centers to laboratories. If an unreliable cold chain or significant transportation delays (greater than 3–4 days) are anticipated, 1% cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) should be added to the sputum in a volume roughly equal to the sputum sample. However, CPC-treated samples should not be refrigerated, as low temperatures may cause crystallization and inactivation. CPC-treated sputum can only be cultured on egg-based media, not liquid or agar media. Molecular tests like Xpert MTB/RIF and line probe assays yield reliable results with CPC-treated sputum, and these samples can be tested for up to one month if stored and transported at ambient temperature. Each sputum container must be labeled with the patient’s unique survey identification number (not on the lid), and the same identification number should be used on sputum collection and laboratory request forms. Standard laboratory forms accompanying sputum specimens during shipment and for requesting laboratory analysis should be modified as necessary for the survey. To ensure traceability, health centers should maintain a register documenting the survey identification number, dates of sample collection, shipment, receipt of laboratory results, and transmission of results to the patient. Diagnostic testing algorithms defined during the survey planning phase must be strictly followed. For culture-based surveys, sputum decontamination serves two purposes: eliminating non-mycobacterial bacteria and homogenizing the sample. The goal is to destroy as much contaminating flora as possible while preserving mycobacteria. The Petroff method, using a final sodium hydroxide (NaOH) concentration of up to 2%, is widely preferred. If CPC was used for transport, NaOH decontamination should only be applied if the delay between sample collection and processing exceeds one week, with a reduced contact time of 5–10 minutes. For liquid culture, the preferred decontamination method is N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NALC)-NaOH. Sputum specimens should be refrigerated at +4°C before processing at the reference laboratory, and bacteriological examination should be conducted as soon as possible. CPC-treated specimens should not be refrigerated. Before inoculating media, CPC-treated specimens should be centrifuged without cooling, and the liquid should be decanted as much as possible. Solid and liquid culture and identification should follow WHO recommendations. All positive cultures must be stored in a deep freezer at -20°C or lower until retesting at the Supranational Reference Laboratory (SRL) is completed or the strain is excluded from further testing. Sputum sediments and microscopy slides should also be stored until final culture and drug susceptibility testing (DST) results are available. All procedures involving specimen handling for culture and DST must be conducted in high-risk TB laboratories, as defined in the WHO Tuberculosis Laboratory Biosafety Manual. Special precautions are necessary when opening, closing, or shaking bottles and during centrifugation, as these activities may generate infectious aerosols. The transportation of TB cultures poses significant risks in the event of accidents or container breakage. Therefore, the exchange of strains between the Central Reference Laboratory and the SRL must adhere to regulations outlined in Annex 7. Susceptibility testing should be performed on a single isolate per patient. Participating laboratories should use the WHO-recommended method with which they are most familiar to minimize variability. Laboratories must demonstrate proficiency by participating in at least one round of DST proficiency testing with an SRL before the survey. If the proportion of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) cases is low, all MDR-TB strains and 1–2 susceptible strains enrolled immediately after each MDR-TB patient should be retested. If MDR-TB cases are numerous, retesting 10–30% of MDR-TB strains and 1–2 consecutive susceptible strains may be more feasible. If DST for second-line drugs is unavailable in the country or if laboratory performance standards are unknown, testing can be conducted at an SRL outside the country, provided sufficient resources are allocated to cover costs. Molecular-based surveys can incorporate any WHO-endorsed laboratory test. Unlike culture-based methods, some molecular tests, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, can be performed at district or sub-district levels, reducing logistical challenges associated with sample transport and processing. A monitoring schedule should be developed for all participating health facilities. A checklist can help assess staff adherence to survey protocols, including patient inclusion/exclusion criteria, safe sputum collection and transport, and traceability of samples and results. Missing information should be promptly requested from respective centers. Supervisory visits should target facilities with low patient enrollment, incomplete data collection, or delays in sample shipment. Midterm review meetings should evaluate data quality, laboratory procedures, and preliminary survey results. External monitoring by independent experts is also recommended. Data management aims to produce high-quality data on individual characteristics and aggregated indicators, such as the proportion of MDR-TB cases. A database manager should oversee the development of a centrally managed database. If expertise is unavailable, external partners should be consulted. A data management plan should outline procedures for accurate, complete, and verifiable data collection, handling, validation, and analysis. All enrolled patients, including those with lost or contaminated samples, must be entered into the database. Unique survey identification numbers should be used consistently across all forms and databases to ensure data linkage. Barcode labels and handheld scanners are recommended to reduce transcription errors.
